title: This Tiny Snake Escapes Danger by Rolling Like a Wheel
summary:
Snakes have many ways to escape danger. Some bite, some rattle their tails, and some even spit venom. But the dwarf reed snake of Southeast Asia has an especially surprising trick: when it feels threatened, it rolls away like a speeding wheel.

An adult dwarf reed snake is usually less than 12 inches long. Yet by rolling, it can move as fast as one foot per second. That is about four times faster than it travels by slithering. And it is not a wild, flailing escape. The snake can roll along a straight path while keeping its head steady and facing forward.

Scientists at Toho University in Japan wanted to know how it does this. They filmed the snakes with high-speed cameras, which can show fast movements in slow motion. They shared what they learned in a study in the journal Current Biology.

The team found that the snake does not spin its whole body in one simple motion. Instead, it whips one side of its body forward toward the ground while a curved part swings down near its head. The researchers call each of these movements a "stroke." The snake then switches between its left and right sides with each stroke.

It is a bit like twirling a rope in a circle while holding one end in your hand. In this case, the end being held still is the snake's head. This lets the snake keep its eyes and other senses upright and pointed ahead, even while it moves quickly.

The study also shows that it is hard to guess what an animal can do just by looking at its body. A snake may be built to slither, but it can still get creative.
why_it_matters: The study shows that animals can do things we would never guess from their body shape, which reminds scientists to observe carefully instead of assuming.

Small animals that many predators hunt often develop special escape tricks, such as playing dead, jumping or rolling away.
A snake's head holds its eyes and other sense organs, so keeping the head steady helps it see where it is going.
